## Summary

  The race-test job for Go 1.22 on macos-latest is failing with:

  dyld[11114]: missing LC_UUID load command in /private/var/folders/.../go-yaml.test
  dyld[11114]: missing LC_UUID load command
  signal: abort trap
  FAIL  github.com/goccy/go-yaml        0.003s

  This is visible on PR #889 but is unrelated to that PR's changes — it reproduces on the current master as well.

## Cause

  GitHub recently updated macos-latest to macOS 26 (image macos-26-arm64/20260630). macOS 26 enforces the presence of the LC_UUID Mach-O load command in binaries. Go's linker did not start emitting LC_UUID until Go 1.23 (https://go.dev/issue/68678), so any test binary built with Go 1.21 or
  1.22 is immediately killed by dyld on macOS 26.

  Go 1.23 and 1.24 jobs pass fine. The Go 1.21 job on macOS happened to get cancelled before it could hit the same crash, but it would also fail.

##  Reproduction

  On any macOS 26 machine with Go 1.22.12 installed:

  $ go1.22.12 test ./...
  dyld[52691]: missing LC_UUID load command in .../go-yaml.test
  signal: abort trap
  FAIL  github.com/goccy/go-yaml        0.447s

##  Suggested fix

  Remove Go 1.21 and 1.22 from the macos-latest matrix in .github/workflows/go.yml, or pin those jobs to an older macOS runner image (e.g. macos-13). The Ubuntu and Windows jobs for Go 1.21/1.22 are unaffected and can remain.

**Describe the bug**

`yaml.Unmarshal` produces different results for `? >0` depending on whether a trailing newline is present. Without a newline it parses successfully as a mapping with key `>0`. With a newline it fails, interpreting `>0` as a block scalar header.

**To Reproduce**

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	goyaml "github.com/goccy/go-yaml"
)

func main() {
	var v1, v2 any

	// Without trailing newline — succeeds
	err1 := goyaml.Unmarshal([]byte("? >0"), &v1)
	fmt.Printf("without newline: %v (err: %v)\n", v1, err1)

	// With trailing newline — fails
	err2 := goyaml.Unmarshal([]byte("? >0\n"), &v2)
	fmt.Printf("with newline:    %v (err: %v)\n", v2, err2)
}
```

Output:
```
without newline: map[>0:<nil>] (err: <nil>)
with newline:    map[:<nil>] (err: [1:3] invalid header option: "0"
>  1 | ? >0
         ^
)
```

**Expected behavior**

Both inputs should parse identically. `>0` here follows the `?` explicit key indicator and should be treated as a plain scalar value, not a block scalar header. A trailing newline should not change how the token is classified.

**Version Variables**
- Go version: 1.26.3
- go-yaml's Version: v1.19.2

**Additional context**

We encountered this while building a YAML formatting tool that appends a final newline to files (standard practice). Files containing explicit key indicators with values that resemble block scalar headers become unparseable after the newline is added.
title: Trailing newline changes parse result for explicit key with `>` value

**Note: This issue is a proposal for a pair of backwards-compatible behavior changes and an offer to volunteer to do the work should it be agreeable to the project maintainer(s).**

> **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

When using `yaml.CustomUnmarshaler[T any](unmarshaler func(*T, []byte) error)` to unmarshal custom struct types the `[]byte` slice can contain quotes, such as `"` or `'`, used to wrap the string value. I consider this to be intended behavior even though it is often inconvenient as there may be reasons to want the quotes when decoding.

Additionally, multi-line strings are provided to the unmarshalling function as-is, and contain the indicator used to declare the block. This may be desirable for some circumstances, but does not seem intuitive (or a good developer experience) when using a higher-level library APIs like `Decoder.Decode(v interface{})`.

Ultimately each custom unmarshalling function must be written to contend with the raw bytes of a YAML node when (I believe) a common, desired use case is to take a value that the YAML specification considers a string and unmarshal it *after* quotes and/or block indicators have been stripped away.

> **Describe the solution you'd like**

**Changes to current default behaviors:**

1. Automatically remove the `"` and `'` characters from scalar node values that the YAML specification either considers a string (as in, tagged as `!!str`) or that the user considers a string (such as an untagged, but quoted string value) _prior_ to calling custom unmarshalling functions.
2. Strip block indicators, [as well as the initial and trailing newlines](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#block-folding), for multi-line node values (tagged or not) that are always considered strings, _prior_ to calling custom unmarshalling functions.

**Additions to the library:**

1. Introduce a `DecodeOption` that re-enables the current behavior of including double and single quotes to customer unmarshalling functions.
2. Introduce a `DecodeOption` that re-enables the current behavior of including multi-line string indicators to customer unmarshalling functions.

> **Describe alternatives you've considered**

**Assumptions made in this proposal:**

- The raw content of a quoted strings in a YAML node are always intended to be the equivalent of a Go `string` prior to unmarshalling.
- Unquoted, multi-line strings "[plain style](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#double-quoted-style)" blocks can never be interpreted as anything other than a string. This means that 

**Proposed alternatives:**

Only implement the behavior change for multi-line strings, and leave the existing behavior regarding quotes unchanged.

> **Additional context**

- The changes in this proposal are considered backwards compatible for code that strips away double-quotes, single-quotes, leading or trailing newlines, and  multi-line indicators as those activities are usually no-ops if the content is not present in the `[]byte` slice.
- The [YAML specification](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/) v1.2.2 was consulted, but not exhaustively, when preparing this issue.
- This issue was written after reviewing all of the [existing issues](https://github.com/goccy/go-yaml/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20quote) returned for the search `is:issue quote`.
- *No generative AI was used to create this issue* (sadly, I feel the need to say this due to my writing style).

## Describe the bug

When a YAML stream contains a "comment-only document" between two `---` separators (a document whose body is nothing but comments and blank lines), `parser.ParseBytes` silently drops the document that follows it. The resulting `*ast.File.Docs` contains fewer documents than the source implies, and the trailing content is lost with no error.

The number of documents returned is `(actual document count) - 1` for each comment-only document in the stream.

This was observed on goccy/go-yaml **v1.19.2** (latest at time of report), and does not occur with `gopkg.in/yaml.v3`, which parses the same input as the expected number of documents (the middle one having a nil / empty body).

## To Reproduce

Minimal reproducer — three logical documents separated by `---`, where the middle document has only a comment:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/goccy/go-yaml/parser"
)

func main() {
	src := []byte("a: 1\n---\n# comment only\n---\nb: 2\n")
	file, err := parser.ParseBytes(src, 0)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Println("parse error:", err)
		return
	}
	fmt.Printf("docs: %d\n", len(file.Docs))
	for i, d := range file.Docs {
		fmt.Printf("  [%d] bodyNil=%v\n", i, d.Body == nil)
	}
}
```

Observed output:

```
docs: 2
  [0] bodyNil=false
  [1] bodyNil=true
```

The `b: 2` document is silently absent from `file.Docs`.

Comparable minimal cases that all exhibit the drop (the common pattern is a non-empty document preceded or followed by a comment-only document between separators):

- `a: 1\n---\n# comment only\n---\nb: 2\n` → 2 docs (expected 3)
- `a: 1\n---\n# just\n# comments\n---\nb: 2\n` → 2 docs (expected 3)
- `a: 1\n---\n\n# leading blank + comment\n\n---\nb: 2\n` → 2 docs (expected 3)

For contrast, these parse as expected:

- `a: 1\n---\nb: 2\n` → 2 docs (no comment-only doc; no drop).
- `a: 1\n---\nb: 2\n---\n` → 3 docs (trailing empty allowed).

## Expected behavior

`parser.ParseBytes` should return one `*ast.DocumentNode` for every `---`-separated segment in the source, regardless of whether a segment contains only comments or blank lines. The comment-only document can have a `Body` of `nil` (or a suitable empty-content representation), but the document that follows it must not be consumed or elided.

Concretely for the reproducer above:

```
docs: 3
  [0] bodyNil=false   # a: 1
  [1] bodyNil=true    # the comment-only doc
  [2] bodyNil=false   # b: 2
```

This matches `gopkg.in/yaml.v3`'s behavior for the same input and matches YAML 1.2 §9.1 ("A YAML stream consists of zero or more documents"), which does not treat a comment-only document as a continuation of the next.

## Version Variables

- Go version: 1.26.2
- go-yaml's Version: v1.19.2

## Additional context

We hit this in a project fixture during a migration from `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` to `goccy/go-yaml`. The affected fixture had a narrative comment block sandwiched between `---` separators that explained a change; the comment was preserved for future readers. Under goccy, the document that followed the comment block silently stopped loading — the engine couldn't find its content at test time, with no parse error to indicate what happened.

We've added an in-project guard that counts `---` separators and compares against the non-empty document count from `file.Docs`; when the parser's count is lower, we surface an author-facing error naming the "remove redundant `---` around comment-only docs" remediation. The guard has proven useful independent of this bug — any similar silent multi-doc issue would also be caught — but the underlying parser behavior would be good to fix upstream so ruleset authors don't need the guard at all.

Happy to provide a larger real-world fixture, contribute a regression test, or attempt a patch if you would like. Thank you!
title: goccy/go-yaml drops documents after comment-only documents in multi-doc streams

## Problem 
Currently, during unmarshalling, certain type mismatches are handled inconsistently:

Non-convertible types (e.g., "abc" → int32) correctly return an error
However, lossy numeric mismatches (e.g., 0.5 → int32) are silently ignored, leaving the field with a value which was not intended. (0)

This can lead to silent data loss, especially in configuration-driven systems where YAML is commonly used. For example:
```
quota:
  int: 0.5
  float: 0.5
```
With a struct:
```
type Quota struct {
    Int   int32   `yaml:"int"`
    Float float32 `yaml:"float"`
}
```

The int field is silently set to 0 without any error, while float is parsed correctly. This makes it difficult to detect misconfigurations and can lead to subtle bugs in production systems.

## Solution

Introduce an optional strict decoding mode that enforces stronger type safety for integer values during unmarshalling.

For example:
```
dec := yaml.NewDecoder(r)
dec.StrictIntTypes(true)
```
In strict mode:

- Any lossy type mismatch (including numeric conversions like float → int) should return an error
- No fields should be silently skipped
- Decoding should fail fast on the first violation

This would allow users to opt into schema-like validation behaviour while preserving the current permissive default.

### Alternatives Considered
- Implementing custom UnmarshalYAML methods for strict validation
- Performing a two-phase decode (map[string]interface{} → manual validation → struct)
- Adding post-unmarshal validation logic

While these approaches work, they:

- Add boilerplate and duplication
- Push validation responsibility to application code
- Reduce the benefits of using a strongly typed struct during decoding

A built-in strict mode would provide a cleaner and more consistent solution.

## Additional context

YAML is often used for configuration in production systems where correctness is critical. Silent field drops due to type mismatches can be difficult to debug and may lead to unintended behavior.

Other ecosystems (e.g., JSON schema validators, Protobuf) tend to favor fail-fast behavior for type mismatches. Providing an opt-in strict mode would make go-yaml more suitable for these use cases without breaking backward compatibility.

Additionally, it may be useful to consider:

- Clearer error messages that include full field paths (e.g., quota.int)
- Optional detection of lossy assignments (e.g., float → int) even outside strict mode
title: Strict type enforcement for integer values during YAML unmarshal to prevent silent data loss

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

When working with YAML configuration files that contain URLs, I have to manually parse `url.URL` fields from strings. Unlike `time.Duration`, which is natively supported by the decoder/encoder, `url.URL` requires a custom unmarshaler on every struct that contains a URL field.

For example, this does not work today:

```go
type Config struct {
    Endpoint url.URL `yaml:"endpoint"`
}

var cfg Config
yaml.Unmarshal([]byte(`endpoint: https://example.com/api`), &cfg)
// error: cannot unmarshal string into url.URL
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Add native encode/decode support for `net/url.URL`, following the same pattern used for `time.Duration` (added in #201).

- **Decode**: parse YAML string values into `url.URL` using `url.Parse()`
- **Encode**: serialize `url.URL` values using `url.URL.String()`
- Support both `url.URL` and `*url.URL`

Expected behavior:

```go
type Config struct {
    Endpoint url.URL  `yaml:"endpoint"`
    Callback *url.URL `yaml:"callback"`
}

var cfg Config
yaml.Unmarshal([]byte(`
endpoint: https://example.com/api
callback: https://example.com/callback
`), &cfg)
// cfg.Endpoint.Host == "example.com"
// cfg.Callback.Host == "example.com"

yaml.Unmarshal([]byte(`endpoint: https://example.com/api`), &cfg)
// cfg.Callback == nil (pointer type is nil when omitted)
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Implementing `yaml.Unmarshaler` on a wrapper type around `url.URL` for each struct — works but adds boilerplate to every project.
- Using a plain `string` field and calling `url.Parse()` after unmarshaling — loses the benefit of typed configuration.

**Additional context**

[]

**Describe the bug**
Since v1.13.0, strings that start with a colon (`:`) are no longer quoted during marshaling. This causes compatibility issues with Ruby's YAML parser (Psych), which interprets unquoted strings starting with `:` as Ruby Symbols.

**To Reproduce**
 [Go Playground](https://go.dev/play/p/MocGao5QkPY)
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/goccy/go-yaml"
	"github.com/goccy/go-yaml/token"
)

func main() {
	// Check if quoting is needed
	fmt.Printf("token.IsNeedQuoted(%q) = %v\n", ":0", token.IsNeedQuoted(":0"))
	fmt.Printf("token.IsNeedQuoted(%q) = %v\n", ":8080", token.IsNeedQuoted(":8080"))

	// Marshal example
	data := map[string]string{
		"LISTEN_ADDR": ":0",
		"OTHER_PORT":  ":8080",
	}

	output, _ := yaml.Marshal(data)
	fmt.Println(string(output))
}
```

**Output in v1.12.0 (correct):**

```
token.IsNeedQuoted(":0") = true
token.IsNeedQuoted(":8080") = true
LISTEN_ADDR: ":0"
OTHER_PORT: ":8080"
```

**Output in v1.19.1 (current - incorrect):**

```
token.IsNeedQuoted(":0") = false
token.IsNeedQuoted(":8080") = false
LISTEN_ADDR: :0
OTHER_PORT: :8080
```


**Expected behavior**
```
token.IsNeedQuoted(":0") = true
token.IsNeedQuoted(":8080") = true
LISTEN_ADDR: ":0"
OTHER_PORT: ":8080"
```

**Screenshots**
If applicable, add screenshots to help explain your problem.

**Version Variables**
 - Go version: 1.25
 - go-yaml's Version: v1.19.1

**Additional context**
**The Problem**

When Ruby's YAML parser reads the unquoted output, it misinterprets the values:

```ruby
require 'yaml'

yaml_content = <<-YAML
LISTEN_ADDR: :0
OTHER_PORT: :8080
YAML

parsed = YAML.safe_load(yaml_content, permitted_classes: [Symbol])

addr = parsed["LISTEN_ADDR"]
puts "Type: #{addr.class}"      # => Symbol
puts "Value: #{addr.to_s}"      # => "0" (colon is lost!)

port = parsed["OTHER_PORT"]
puts "Type: #{port.class}"      # => Symbol  
puts "Value: #{port.to_s}"      # => "8080" (colon is lost!)
```

In Ruby/YAML, `:value` syntax represents a Symbol. When a Symbol is converted to a string, it loses the leading colon. This breaks applications expecting the original string value.

**Root Cause**

This regression was introduced in commit [83d3e55](https://github.com/goccy/go-yaml/commit/83d3e55c2408552b08bd69ac9b0b5f6d6e47d9d7) ("Fix quotation for timestamps #515").

The change replaced `looksLikeTimeValue()` with `isTimestamp()`:

**Before (v1.12.0):**

```go
func looksLikeTimeValue(value string) bool {
    for i, c := range value {
        switch c {
        case ':', '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9':
            continue
        case '0':
            if i == 0 {
                return false
            }
            continue
        }
        return false
    }
    return true  // ":0" matches this pattern → quoted
}
```

**After (v1.13.0+):**

```go
func isTimestamp(value string) bool {
    for _, format := range timestampFormats {
        if _, err := time.Parse(format, value); err == nil {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false  // ":0" is not a valid timestamp → not quoted
}
```

The old heuristic accidentally provided correct behavior for values starting with `:`. The new implementation, while more accurate for timestamps, broke quoting for these values.

**Real-World Use Case: GitLab CI Configuration**

We use goccy/go-yaml to generate `.gitlab-ci.yml` files. A common pattern for CI tests is to bind servers to a random available port:

```yaml
variables:
  INTERNAL_SERVER_LISTEN_ADDR: ":0"
```

The value `:0` means "listen on all interfaces, let the OS assign an available port" — a standard Go/network convention.

After upgrading from v1.12.0 to v1.19.0, the generated YAML became:

```yaml
variables:
  INTERNAL_SERVER_LISTEN_ADDR: :0
```

GitLab CI (which uses Ruby) interprets `:0` as a Symbol, converting it to the string `"0"` when passed as an environment variable. This causes our application to fail:

```
panic: listen tcp: address 0: missing port in address
```

**Affected Ecosystem**

Many tools in the DevOps ecosystem use Ruby-based YAML parsers (Psych):

- **GitLab CI/CD**
- **GitHub Actions** (some components)
- **Chef**
- **Puppet**
- **Vagrant**
- **Homebrew**
- **CocoaPods**
- **Fastlane**

YAML files generated by goccy/go-yaml may be consumed by any of these tools, making Ruby compatibility important.

**YAML Specification Note**

While `:0` is technically valid unquoted YAML 1.2, Ruby's YAML parser follows YAML 1.1 conventions where `:value` represents a Symbol. Quoting such values ensures cross-parser compatibility.

**Suggested Fix**

Add `:` to the first-character check in `IsNeedQuoted()` in `token/token.go`:

```go
first := value[0]
switch first {
case '*', '&', '[', '{', '}', ']', ',', '!', '|', '>', '%', '\'', '"', '@', ' ', '`', ':':
    //                                                                              ^^^
    return true
}
```

This ensures strings starting with `:` are always quoted, maintaining compatibility with Ruby YAML parsers while having no negative impact on Go consumers (quoted strings are parsed identically).

**Describe the bug**
When decoding YAML into structs containing nested pointer fields, goccy/go-yaml does not automatically allocate nil pointer-to-struct fields, while Go’s standard encoding/json (and sigs.k8s.io/yaml) do. sigs.k8s.io/yaml uses gopkg.in/yaml.v3 under the hood.

This results in surprising behavior when reusing the same structs for both JSON and YAML — nested pointer fields remain nil after unmarshalling, even though the YAML contains valid data.

**To Reproduce**
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/goccy/go-yaml"
)

type Inner struct {
	Field string `json:"field"`
}

type Outer struct {
	Inner *Inner `json:"inner"`
}

func main() {
	yml := `
inner:
  field: hello
`

	var o Outer
	if err := yaml.Unmarshal([]byte(yml), &o); err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("%#v\n", o.Inner)
}
```
*Actual output*
`(*main.Inner)(nil)`
*Expected output*
`&main.Inner{Field:"hello"}`

**Expected behavior**
Preallocate pointers

**Version Variables**
 - Go version: [e.g. 1.25 ]
 - go-yaml's Version: [e.g. v1.18.0 ]

**Suggested solution**
Introduce a new decode option:
`yaml.NewDecoder(r, yaml.AutoAllocatePointers())`
When enabled, automatically allocate nil pointer fields during unmarshal if the YAML node is a mapping/object.
This would match encoding/json semantics and improve compatibility.

OR

Make this the default behavior, since it aligns with standard Go expectations (and avoids subtle bugs).

Hi @shuheiktgw!

I’ve been testing this further after your suggestion of storing the original `ValidationErrors` via a custom validator.
What I’m noticing is that, with the current logic in the library, I would still need to handle two different cases in my code for what is essentially the same validation scenario, I'm not sure it's a bug or not.

Take the case of a required `bar` field. In case the field is nested:

```yaml

   bar: ""
```

It returns a `yaml.SyntaxError`.

comments.body:
👋 Thank you for reporting the issue! I took the time to investigate it, and here's what I found. The problem arises because we currently [create a new map](https://github.com/goccy/go-yaml/blob/25e5d9094248e480434ca87d9119e3d9ce7ac1d7/decode.go#L1714) and [assign it back to the destination](https://github.com/goccy/go-yaml/blob/25e5d9094248e480434ca87d9119e3d9ce7ac1d7/decode.go#L1782) when unmarshaling a map. If `yaml.Unmarshal` is called within a function or method, the caller cannot access the newly created map since it's only assigned to a local variable inside that function or method.

If we want to align the behavior with `gopkg.in/yaml.v3`, the fix is relatively straightforward — instead of creating and assigning a new map, we could modify the existing one in place. However, I’m hesitant to make that change for the following reasons:

1. **Behavioral changes that are not backward-compatible**: For example, with this change, the provided map would retain its original entries, which it currently doesn't. It could also retain partial results in case unmarshaling fails.
2. **Inconsistent behavior in `gopkg.in/yaml.v3`**: Specifically, the library also fails to update slices when `Unmarshal` is called within a function or method — which is consistent with how `goccy/go-yaml` behaves. In my opinion, the behavior of `goccy/go-yaml` is actually more consistent overall.

#805 is the same problem

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
I'm looking at migrating [SOPS](https://github.com/getsops/sops) to goccy/go-yaml. For that I need to be able to parse arbitrary YAML documents and process its structure without assumptions on how it should looks like. While playing around with `parser.ParseBytes()` and the resulting AST, I noticed that I don't know how to figure out whether something that ends up as a `StringNode` is actually a string, or something else (date/timestamp, integer, float):
```yaml
examples:
  - 2024-01-01  # a YAML date
  - 2001-12-15T02:59:43.1Z  # a YAML timestamp
  - 0x123982139013098129831983AB1231231312  # hexadecimal integer
  - 98123918398129831987841872387138712837  # an integer
  - 0o012345670123456701234567  # an octal integer
  - 2.0e308  # a floating point number
  - foo  # an actual string
```
All the above sequence entries result in a `StringNode`. If you quote all the above numbers with `"..."`, then you also get `StringNode`s with the same values. I don't see how to figure out from a `StringNode` whether it actually represents a string, or real data (like a date, timestamp, large integer, large float).

What gopkg.in/yaml.v3 does:
- Dates and timestamps are parsed as `time.Time` objects.
- The large decimal integer (`98123918398129831987841872387138712837`) is parsed as a floating point number (distorting the value).
- Everything else is treated as a string. (With the same problems that I mentioned above.)

**Describe the solution you'd like**
**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I'm not sure what the best way to proceed is. The numbers above have been picked so that they cannot be parsed as Golang integers or floats. (The date, and timestamps in general, can be represented by Golang types.)

Maybe:
1. One (or two) new node type(s) for dates/timestamps? (Depending on whether dates and timestamps should be treated separately. gopkg.in/yaml.v3 simply uses `time.Time` to represent all dates and timestamps.)
2. Add extra data to the `StringNode` which tells what the data actually is (actual string; date/timestamp; integer; hexadecimal integer; octal integer; floating point number) if there is no native representation.
3. Maybe even have an option to parse all values (integers, floats, bools, NaN/Infinity, ...) as `StringNode` with type info? (That would allow lossless transformations of floats, for example, allowing to distinguish between `1.10` and `1.1`.)

(Obviously all three can also be implemented together. I'm currently tending to like 2. and 3. most.)

Ref: https://github.com/getsops/sops/issues/1616

Also, you can directly decode into a specified Go value using `yaml.Unmarshal` or `yaml.NewDecoder`. If you prefer to use parser.ParseBytes manually, you can decode an `ast.File` to convert it into Go types. Since both `ast.File` and `ast.Node` implement the `io.Reader` interface, they can be passed as arguments to the NewDecoder function.

to get hold of the value - it will be of type `bool`, `int`, `float64`, `string`, or `time.Time`. gopkg.in/yaml.v3 also does not allow me to distinguish between strings and large ints/floats that cannot be parsed into Golang ints/floats, but it does allow me to identify dates/timestamps (I cannot distinguish between timestamps and dates though, which is also a problem).

With goccy/go-yaml, I don't see how I can get that information from `ast.Node`. Large ints/strings and timestamps and dates are parsed as an `ast.StringNode`, and there is no information on whether it was actually a string (for example because it was quoted), or whether it was a large integer or float or date/timestamp that goccy/go-yaml simply didn't parse.

So, given a `StringNode` with value `12398132981498123981`, how do I know whether this corresponds to an integer, or a string? Or if it has value `2024-01-01`, how do I know whether it corresponds to a date, or a string? In YAML the distinction is very clear:
```yaml
- 12398132981498123981  # integer
- "12398132981498123981"  # string
- 2024-01-01  # date
- "2024-01-01"  # string
```
But goccy/go-yaml's `StringNode` makes it hard to know that information. The only way I see right now is to parse `StringNode.Token.Origin` and basically manually re-do what goccy/go-yaml is doing.

Ok, I think I figured out how to distinguish a `node` of type `ast.StringNode` that's a quoted string from a string that could be a date/timestamp/integer/float: `node.Token.Type == token.SingleQuoteType || node.Token.Type == token.DoubleQuoteType` checks whether it was quoted. If it wasn't quoted, I need to check whether it's actually an integer, float, date, or timestamp that wasn't parsed.
@felixfontein Yes, if you just need to determine whether it's a quoted string, that approach will work fine.

In case anyone has a similar problem, the following documents contain regular expressions that match all strings representing integers, floating point numbers, and timestamps supported by YAML:
- https://yaml.org/type/int.html
- https://yaml.org/type/float.html
- https://yaml.org/type/timestamp.html

I'm a bit torn about sexagesimal support. gopkg.in/yaml.v3, goccy/go-yaml, and ruamel.yaml do not seem to support it, though PyYAML does. (I guess it didn't always support it.)

Determining the Go's type at the ast.Node level is not a common approach, so if you want to do it manually, you will need to implement the type-checking logic yourself.

comments.body: I see the same issue as well.

I ran into the same issue and traced the root cause in detail.

The bug is a mismatch between `MappingValueNode.Replace` and `LiteralNode.String()`:

1. `MappingValueNode.Replace` computes a column delta and calls `value.AddColumn(delta)`, which shifts `Position.Column` on the replacement node's tokens.
2. `LiteralNode.String()` ignores `Position.Column` entirely and returns the raw `Origin` text (verbatim scanner bytes) instead.
3. `StringNode.String()`, by contrast, correctly uses `Position.Column` to rebuild indented output.

This means `AddColumn` shifts metadata that `LiteralNode.String()` never reads. The `Origin` retains the indentation from the source document (the replacement), not the destination. The number of characters eaten from each line equals the column delta.

A minimal reproduction that shows the issue even without YAML-special characters:

```go
data := []byte("spec:\n  content: |\n    old content\n    second line\n")
file, _ := parser.ParseBytes(data, parser.ParseComments)
path, _ := goyaml.PathString("$.spec.content")

valBytes, _ := goyaml.MarshalWithOptions("new line 1\nnew line 2\n", goyaml.UseLiteralStyleIfMultiline(true))
valFile, _ := parser.ParseBytes(valBytes, 0)

tmp := &ast.File{Docs: []*ast.DocumentNode{file.Docs[0]}}
path.ReplaceWithNode(tmp, valFile.Docs[0].Body)
file.Docs[0] = tmp.Docs[0]

fmt.Println(file.String())
// "new " is eaten from each line: outputs "line 1" and "line 2" instead of "new line 1" and "new line 2"
```

A potential fix would be to make `LiteralNode.String()` delegate to `n.Value.String()` (`StringNode.String()`) which already handles position-based indentation correctly, rather than using raw `Origin`.

body:
When source containing Windows line endings is tokenized, the line numbers can be incorrect.

Given this file:

```
# a
# b
# c
```

This list of tokens is generated:

```
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" a" [ORG]:"# a\r" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 1:1:0:1
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" b" [ORG]:"\n# b\r" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 3:1:0:5
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" c" [ORG]:"\n# c\r" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 5:1:0:9
```

Note that each line is numbered `1`,`3`, and `5` respectively.

With Windows line endings replaced with Unix line endings, the lines are numbered correctly:

```
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" a" [ORG]:"# a\n" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 1:1:0:1
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" b" [ORG]:"# b\n" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 2:1:0:4
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" c" [ORG]:"# c\n" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 3:1:0:7
```

You can add Windows line endings by running this sed expression against the input file:

```
sed -i -e 's/$/\r/' file
```

And remove them with this:


```
sed -i -e 's/\r$//' file
```

Code to reproduce:

```go
tokens := lexer.Tokenize(src)
tokens.Dump()
```

comments.body:
Upon further investigation it looks like this only occurs due to the way comments are scanned.

https://github.com/goccy/go-yaml/blob/f4ccce9f01a41e6da7dfbfad021f1f96afbbb76f/scanner/scanner.go#L660-L675

When a `\r` rune is encountered, it is immediately considered a newline and the line is progressed, even though the following `\n` is also part of the CRLF sequence. Removing `\r` from the case resolves this bug.

```
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" a\r" [ORG]:"# a\r\n" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 1:1:0:1
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" b\r" [ORG]:"# b\r\n" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 2:1:0:5
- [TYPE]:"Comment" [CHARTYPE]:"Indicator" [INDICATOR]:"Comment" [VALUE]:" c\r" [ORG]:"# c\r\n" [POS(line:column:level:offset)]: 3:1:0:9
```

# What
It might be nice to be able to add 'remain' flag as a struct tag to `MapSlice` type fields, and unmarshal key-values in yaml which are not defined in struct fields.

# Example
```
type A struct {
 	Name struct
 	Options yaml.MapSlice `yaml:"-,remain"`
 }
 
 var data = `
 name: sheep
 age: 20
 occupation:
 	category: engineer
 	company: qwerty
 `
 func main() {
 	a := A{}
 	_ := yaml.Unmarshal([]byte(data), &a)
 	fmt.Println(a) // {sheep [{age 20} {occupation [{category engineer} {company qwerty}]}]}
 }
```

# Why
In case you have small set of required configs and large set of optional configs in yaml, it is troublesome to define all optional item as struct fields. Additionally such optional items are liable to change, so I found it more useful to get as MapSlice together.
